prize_parts.citation: For introducing firm heterogeneity and selection into the theory of international trade, and for showing how selection into exporting and foreign investment and reallocation across firms shape the gains from trade.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: B001 alone, with Helpman and Melitz. What changed is how I would word and defend it. The merits are as in round 1. Melitz (2003) and Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple (2004) replaced the representative firm with firms that differ in productivity and sort into exporting or foreign investment. That gave trade a reallocation channel for gains, produced sharp predictions that could be tested in firm-level administrative and customs data, and has been tested in many countries for more than two decades. This is the standard I stated in 2023: a framework together with the data it organises is the contribution. The chair warned that the round-1 convergence comes from shared reasoning patterns, so I tried to find the strongest objections to my own position and not just count agreement. Those objections are about attribution and citation scope, not about whether the discovery is real or mature. I think they are manageable through the citation and the scientific background, because the Committee can credit only the names on the entry. The citation should name selection and reallocation and should not claim settled welfare magnitudes or the whole firm-level trade literature. I would not add a second part. B001 uses two of three laureate slots, and every realistic one-person second part I can see fragments an otherwise coherent credit set.
statement.case_against: The attribution gap is real. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are outside the credited names. Bernard and Jensen's exporter-premia facts motivated the theory, and Eaton-Kortum is a parallel but distinct framework. If the Committee defines the achievement as the whole firm-level trade programme, a two-name award on this entry is too narrow, and Redding's quantitative and spatial claim would rise. The baseline model is rejected in some details, and its welfare implications depend on distributional assumptions, so the lasting value lies partly in the extensions. Krugman's 2008 recognition covers part of the broader lineage, and Helpman's monopolistic-competition foundations sit near it. I think firm selection is a distinct step, but a reasonable member could judge the incremental claim smaller. My judgment depends on reading the discovery as the selection and sorting mechanism, and I cannot settle that from the record. I have not independently verified priority records or citation counts.

responses.point: Enflo says she is less comfortable than others with treating Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum as only a caveat, because if the discovery is the empirical facts plus the theory, the credited names are incomplete. She also says the citation should name selection and firm heterogeneity, not generic trade theory.
responses.response: I agree with the wording point and have adopted it. My citation now names selection into exporting and foreign investment and reallocation across firms. On the attribution point I think she has identified the real fork, and it is a judgement about the unit of discovery, not a fact. My reading is that the prize-worthy unit is the model that turned the exporter-premia facts into a testable mechanism with a new welfare channel. The facts are essential, but they motivated the theory and did not supply the selection and sorting mechanism. I would hold that reading firmly enough to vote on it, but I would not claim it is uncontroversial. If a majority of the Committee read the unit as facts plus theory, I would prefer to see B001 reframed or B006 considered, rather than stretch the credited set.

responses.point: Hassler moved from B006 first to B001 first because B001's discovery boundary and credit story are tighter. He keeps B006 as a credible fallback, and he notes that combining B001 and B006 would exceed three laureates, while a trimmed pairing such as Pakes alone would fragment the BLP credit.
responses.response: I agree that the arithmetic rules out a two-part prize combining B001 with the full B006 credit. A one-person second part, whether Pakes alone from B006 or a single name from B030, splits a credit that is naturally shared, and I would not support it. I also think your move toward B001 reflects the boundary problem and not a lower view of B006's impact. I still think that impact is large and mature. My test for moving B006 above B001 would be a defensible single-discovery boundary, for example demand estimation by Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes alone, plus some evidence on out-of-sample or retrospective validation of structural predictions, since identification there rests heavily on functional-form and instrument assumptions. Without that, B006 stays my second alternative, ahead of nothing and behind B001.

responses.point: Dreber Almenberg holds B030 as an alternative and would define it narrowly around the China-shock evidence rather than merge it with the task framework. She notes that Katz shares his skill-demand work with a 2023 laureate and that the persistence of trade-shock effects is debated.
responses.response: This sharpens my own uncertainty about B030, which is the alternative closest to my field. My opening proposed Autor, Hanson and Katz, and I now think that credit set is hard to defend as one discovery. The skills-and-technology strand and the trade-shock strand rest on different bodies of evidence, and I presented the 2023 prize, so I am aware of how close the skill-demand lineage is to work already recognised. If the Committee turned to B030, I would favour a narrow citation on the labour-market effects of import competition and would want the Katz-versus-Dorn question settled explicitly, not by default. The persistence debate is a real maturity concern that B001 does not share. For that reason B030 remains an alternative and I do not rank it level with B001.

responses.point: Fredriksson says the citation should stay narrow, naming selection and reallocation, and that the credibility of the case rests on testable implications that the data confirmed and refined. He also says the missing empirical pioneers are a recognised limitation, not a reason to widen the award.
responses.response: I agree with this and rely on the same distinction. The strongest part of the B001 record is that the core selection and sorting predictions were tested repeatedly in microdata. Their partial failures, for example in some distributional and welfare implications, produced extensions that kept the selection logic. I would take your point one step further for the public citation: it should say what was introduced, namely firm heterogeneity and selection, and leave the quantitative welfare gains to the scientific background. That wording gives the Committee a candidate that can be defended against the attribution objection without claiming credit for the empirical lineage.

uncertainties: Whether a majority reads the discovery as the selection and sorting mechanism or as the whole firm-level trade programme. This decides whether a two-name award on this entry is adequately credited, and I cannot resolve it from the record.

Whether the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, who are not on the ballot entry, can be handled by citation wording and the scientific background, as I currently judge, or whether it makes the award too narrow.
How far the sensitivity of the welfare conclusions to distributional assumptions should limit the citation. I have limited it to the selection and reallocation mechanism.

Whether a defensible single-discovery boundary exists for B006, and whether there is out-of-sample validation of structural predictions. For B030, whether the task and technology strand and the trade-shock strand can be separated, and how persistent the trade-shock effects are.
Whether Krugman's 2008 recognition makes the incremental step smaller than I judge it to be.
I have not independently verified citation counts, priority claims or award history. My assessment rests on general knowledge and the supplied round-1 files.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to Helpman or Melitz is apparent from my supplied profile. My listed frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler) are not credited on any shortlisted entry. I disclose thematic proximity to B030 through my field of labour economics, and that I presented the 2023 prize to Goldin, which is relevant to the Katz overlap I raise. B030 is an alternative and not my preferred part. I have editorial roles at economics journals, but I identify no tie to credited names from the profile. I disclose these and do not adjudicate them.
